"""French-looking Latin word continuations, plus completion of github.com.

Otherwise predict zero. Within a word, French/English dictionary prefixes
and four-letter spellings supply soft evidence. Familiar French letter
families and place-name endings strengthen a negative prediction, as does
capitalization. This omits individual-name exceptions and amplitudes.
"""
from collections import defaultdict
from functools import lru_cache
from math import log10
import re
import regex
from anyascii import anyascii
from wordfreq import top_n_list, zipf_frequency

READS = ()


def dictionary(language):
    """Collect weighted word starts and four-letter spellings."""
    prefixes = defaultdict(float)
    grams = defaultdict(float)
    for word in top_n_list(language, 100000):
        if not word.isalpha():
            continue
        frequency = 10 ** (zipf_frequency(word, language) - 3)
        word = anyascii(word).lower()
        for end in range(2, len(word) + 1):
            prefixes[word[:end]] += frequency
        for start in range(len(word) - 3):
            grams[word[start:start+4]] += frequency ** 0.5
    return prefixes, grams


FRENCH, ENGLISH = dictionary('fr'), dictionary('en')


def letter_evidence(letters):
    return log10((FRENCH[1].get(letters, 0) + 1) /
                 (ENGLISH[1].get(letters, 0) + 1))


@lru_cache(maxsize=100000)
def spelling(word):
    word = anyascii(word).lower()
    scores = [letter_evidence(word[i:i+4])
              for i in range(len(word) - 3)]
    return sum(scores) / max(1, len(scores))


@lru_cache(maxsize=100000)
def dictionary_evidence(word):
    word = anyascii(word).lower()
    return log10((FRENCH[0].get(word, 0) + .001) /
                 (ENGLISH[0].get(word, 0) + .001))


def positive(x, upper=2):
    return max(0.0, min(upper, x))


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    old = carry[1] if carry is not None and carry[0] == doc else ''
    piece = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    tail = re.search(r'[^\W\d_]+$', piece)
    inside = bool(old and piece and piece[0].isalpha())
    word = (old + piece if inside and piece.isalpha()
            else tail[0] if tail else '')[-80:]
    carry = (doc, word)
    if old.lower() == 'github' and piece == '.com':
        return carry, -1.30
    if not inside or not piece.isalpha() or not regex.fullmatch(r'\p{Latin}+', word):
        return carry, 0.0

    def ends(pattern):
        return bool(re.search(pattern, word, re.I))

    # Four-letter spellings give a soft French-versus-English cue.
    stem = positive(spelling(old))
    whole = positive(spelling(word))
    strength = .193 * whole
    strength += stem * (
        2.586 * ends(r'(?:eau|au)(?:d|t|lt|x)?$')
        + 3.239 * ends(r'gn[aeiouy]?$|[aei]gn$'))
    strength += 3.661 * whole * ends(r'(?:mont|court|ville|bois|bourg)$')
    strength += 1.067 * positive(dictionary_evidence(old), 4) * ends(r'oi(?:s|x)?$')
    strength += old.istitle() * (
        1.025 * ends(r'i(?:er|ers|ere|eres|ère|ères)$')
        + .085 * positive(dictionary_evidence(word), 4))
    return carry, -strength

"""layers.1.mlp.down_proj:4273 — a "word-piece inside a name" component.

What it does, in plain terms: the component is mostly silent. Its clearest behaviour is
negative activation on a *continuation piece* of a Latin-script word: a word that the
tokenizer split into several pieces, on the 2nd, 3rd, ... piece (e.g. "Champign|y",
"Beuch|ot", "Duch|amp", "Chevalier" split as "Cheval|ier"). The strongest cases are rare
proper names and place names (surnames, villages). The sign is almost always negative
there; the size varies a lot from word to word and is not predictable from the token alone.

This program predicts that pattern with two readable rules:
  1. a piece is a continuation piece if it has no leading space, is made of Latin letters,
     and follows a letter piece (so it continues a word);
  2. such a piece is pushed further negative when the word before it is capitalised
     (a name following a name, e.g. "Pierre Beuch|ot").
Everything else is predicted as 0.

It does not know which names are rare, so it captures only the average sign and a little
of the size; a per-word lookup table would capture far more (see the explanation).
"""

READS = ()

LATIN_LIMIT = 0x250  # Basic Latin through Latin Extended-B


def _letters(s):
    s = s.strip()
    return len(s) > 0 and all(ch.isalpha() and ord(ch) < LATIN_LIMIT for ch in s)


def _is_continuation(ts, i):
    """Piece i is a continuation piece: no leading space, Latin letters, after a letter piece."""
    cur = ts[i]
    return i > 0 and not cur.startswith(" ") and _letters(cur) and _letters(ts[i - 1])


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    ts = prefix.token_strings
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    t = len(ts) - 1
    if t < 1 or docs[t] != docs[t - 1] or not _is_continuation(ts, t):
        return carry, 0.0
    # walk back to the first piece of this word, then look at the word before it
    s = t
    while s - 1 >= 0 and docs[s - 1] == docs[t] and _is_continuation(ts, s):
        s -= 1
    before = ts[s - 1].strip() if s - 1 >= 0 and docs[s - 1] == docs[t] else ""
    prev_word_capitalised = before[:1].isupper()
    value = -0.012 - 0.036 * prev_word_capitalised
    return carry, float(value)

"""Layer 1, MLP down_proj, component 4274: a "compound-word tail" detector.

Fires negatively on the tail piece of an English compound noun that the tokenizer split
in two, e.g. "test|bed" (testbed), "Guide|book", "Show|time", "hair|dry|er". The tail must
be letters only, with no leading space, glued to a preceding letter, and be a common
English noun that often ends a compound (bed, book, board, side, top, tape, foot, ...).
Those tails get a strong negative value; other letter-only tails get a weak one.
Inflection pieces (-s, -ed, -ing, -er, ...) get nothing, and so does everything else,
apart from the middle-dot leader run "····", where the repeated "··" token is -1.

Only part of the variance is explained by the word list: the same piece varies with
context (e.g. "bed" is strongest in "/testbed/" paths and weak in "un|bed|ingt").
"""

READS = ()

# Common English nouns that often form the second half of a compound.
HEAD_NOUNS = frozenset(
    """
    site tape guard foot horn fish punk coat gate mill pool side bag hold
    storm person bed cut pack master view boat pot burn fest top wing writer
    back front holder child book mail water work board fruit fold hammer stop
    hub hole watch mix light woman hall wire wall stone plate cap room maker
    drop mate mount dog pit smith club cast hand hill note trip house bird
    pan nut tail team stack star pad kit point seed bridge fire ball bell
    """.split()
)

SUFFIXES = frozenset(
    "s es ed ing er ers ly y ness ment ments tion ion ions al ic ist ism ity ies ied ier iest "
    "ful less able ive ous est ty ur ian ant ent ence ance ize ise en ern ther ture ship hood age".split()
)

HEAD_VALUE = -1.1   # typical activation on a listed compound tail
TAIL_VALUE = -0.05  # other letter-only word tails
DOTS = "··"  # the two-character middle-dot token of a "····" leader run


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    cur = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    same_doc = len(prefix) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2] if same_doc else ""
    if cur == DOTS and prev == DOTS:
        return carry, -1.0
    # A word tail: letters only, no leading space, right after a letter.
    is_tail = cur.isascii() and cur.isalpha() and prev[-1:].isascii() and prev[-1:].isalpha()
    if not is_tail:
        return carry, 0.0
    if cur in HEAD_NOUNS:
        return carry, HEAD_VALUE
    if cur in SUFFIXES or len(cur) < 3:
        return carry, 0.0
    return carry, TAIL_VALUE

"""Attributive particles: a negative response on the word that links a modifier to the
noun it describes.

Main case: the Chinese particle 的 ("de") after a Chinese character, as in 符合条件的人
("people who meet the conditions") or 我的书 ("my book"). Its activation is about -1.6.
The Japanese particles の, 之 (Chinese 之), な and した, and the tokens もの and のお, are
also negative, about -0.8 to -1.2. 的 after a non-Chinese character (a Latin word or a
space) is weaker, about -1.2, and 的 merged into a longer token that starts with it (的人,
的一) is about -1.0. Every other token is predicted as 0.

Only the current token and the one before it are read; there is no state across tokens.
The values are rounded averages over about 7000 training rows. Within 的 the response varies
a lot (std about 1.0) and the preceding tokens do not explain that spread, so the
program predicts the average.
"""
READS = ()

PARTICLES = {
    "的": -1.6,   # Chinese attributive particle, after a Chinese character (see below)
    "の": -1.0,   # Japanese possessive / attributive "no"
    "之": -1.0,   # classical Chinese "zhi", the same role as 的
    "な": -0.8,   # Japanese adjectival "na"
    "した": -0.9,  # Japanese verb ending before a noun
    "もの": -1.1,  # Japanese "mono" after a modifier
    "のお": -1.2,  # Japanese "no" merged with a following character
}
OTHER_DE = -1.2   # 的 after a non-Chinese character
MERGED_DE = -1.0  # a longer token that begins with 的, such as 的人 or 的一


def is_han(ch):
    """True for a common CJK ideograph."""
    return "一" <= ch <= "鿿"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if tok == "的" and prefix.position > 0:
        before = prefix.token_strings[-2][-1:]
        if not (before and is_han(before)):
            return carry, OTHER_DE
    if tok in PARTICLES:
        return carry, PARTICLES[tok]
    if tok.startswith("的"):
        return carry, MERGED_DE
    return carry, 0.0

"""A heuristic for isolated quotation marks and text-span endings.

For double quotes, fitted weights combine attached punctuation, distances from
prior raw and unescaped quotes, and whether an unescaped quote has appeared.
Distances are token counts, measured from document start until a quote appears.
Smaller rules cover apostrophe strings, backticks, comment ends, EOF markers,
some typographic quotes and post-tool role-line breaks. Repeated middle-dot
leaders are inhibited. Ordinary text stays near zero. This is not a full parser;
the scan resets at each document boundary.
"""
import math

READS = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry['doc'] != doc:
        carry = dict(doc=doc, position=0, quote=0, unescaped_quote=0,
                     apostrophe=0, tick=0, comment=0, line=0,
                     seen_unescaped=False, previous='', tail='', slashes=0,
                     last_value=0.0, tool_end=-100)
    c = carry
    t = c['position']
    s = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    p = c['previous']
    tail = c['tail']
    stripped = s.strip()
    newline = '\n' in s
    previous_code_end = p.rstrip()[-1:] in (';', ')', '}', ']')
    after_escaped_newline = tail.endswith('\\n')
    value = -0.003

    if '"' in s:
        q = s.index('"')
        first = not c['seen_unescaped']  # No earlier unescaped double quote.
        raw_gap = max(0.0, math.log1p(t - c['quote']) - 1.5)
        unescaped_gap = max(0.0, math.log1p(t - c['unescaped_quote']) - 1.5)
        comma = ',' in s
        sentence_stop = any(ch in s for ch in '.!?')
        leading = s[:1].isspace()
        key_colon = s[q + 1:].lstrip().startswith(':')
        ending_like = not leading and not key_colon and not any(
            ch.isalnum() for ch in s)
        before_closer = s[q + 1:q + 2] in (';', ')', '}', ']')
        after_closer = q > 0 and s[q - 1] in ';})]'
        code_ending = previous_code_end or after_closer
        # Separation and the local punctuation jointly determine the response.
        value = (0.136
                 + raw_gap * (0.474 * comma
                              + 0.202 * sentence_stop
                              + 0.276 * before_closer
                              - 0.324 * newline)
                 + unescaped_gap * (-0.193 * comma
                                + 0.424 * newline
                                + 0.400 * code_ending * ending_like)
                 + first * (1.004 * newline * ending_like
                            + 1.102 * code_ending * ending_like
                            + 0.497 * stripped.startswith('"')
                            + 0.841 * sentence_stop
                            + 0.705 * comma
                            - 0.346 * leading)
                 + 0.436 * after_escaped_newline)
        value = max(-3.0, min(9.0, value))
    elif stripped in ('EOF', '_EOF'):
        value = 4.3
    elif '*/' in s:
        value = 1.0 if t - c['comment'] > 32 else 0.5
    elif '`' in s:
        if newline and t - c['tick'] > 10:
            value = 1.1
        elif previous_code_end:
            value = 0.8 if t - c['line'] < 18 else 0.1
        elif p.endswith('\n'):
            value = 0.2
        else:
            value = -0.03
    elif "'" in s:
        if after_escaped_newline:
            value = 1.5 if t - c['quote'] < 4 else 0.3
        elif previous_code_end:
            value = 1.0
        elif newline and t - c['apostrophe'] > 8:
            value = 0.4
        else:
            value = 0.0
    elif any(ch in s for ch in '“”„«»「」『』'):
        value = 0.2 if ',' in s else 0.0
    elif s == '\n' and p in ('user', 'assistant', 'system'):
        value = 0.44 if t - c['tool_end'] < 12 else 0.0
    elif newline and p.rstrip().endswith(('"', "'", 'EOF')):
        value = 0.4 * max(0.0, c['last_value'])
    elif stripped and set(stripped) == {'·'} and p.strip() == stripped:
        value = -1.34  # Repeated middle-dot leaders, rather than prose.

    for ch in s:
        if ch == '"':
            c['quote'] = t
            if c['slashes'] % 2 == 0:
                c['unescaped_quote'] = t
                c['seen_unescaped'] = True
        elif ch == "'":
            c['apostrophe'] = t
        elif ch == '`':
            c['tick'] = t
        elif ch == '\n':
            c['line'] = t
        c['slashes'] = c['slashes'] + 1 if ch == '\\' else 0
    if '/*' in s:
        c['comment'] = t
    if '</tool_call>' in s:
        c['tool_end'] = t
    c['tail'] = (tail + s)[-2:]
    c['previous'] = s
    c['position'] = t + 1
    c['last_value'] = float(value)
    return c, float(value)

"""layers.1.mlp.down_proj:4277 — a "closing quote" detector.

What it does: this component writes a bump into the residual stream at the token that CLOSES
a quoted or heredoc string. Its activation is near zero almost everywhere; it is large at:

  * "}}\\n     end of a JSON tool call whose string held code      (about 2.3 after escapes, 1.4 plain)
  * ",  ",\\n  }",  )",   closing quotes of a JSON / code string  (about 2.3 after escapes, 0.3 plain)
  * EOF      end of a shell heredoc                               (about 4)
  * ."  .\\n  !"  ?"      closing quotes of prose sentences          (about 0.3-0.8)

The one thing that raises the value of a closing quote is whether the string it closes held
backslash escapes (\\n, \\"), i.e. code or JSON-escaped text. An escaped closing quote (\\",)
inside such text is pushed slightly negative.

Program: scan the row token by token, track whether we are inside a double-quoted string and
whether that string has contained a backslash, and read the value off a small table of closers.
"""
READS = ()

# Closers whose string held backslash escapes (JSON- or backslash-escaped code).
CLOSE_ESCAPED = {'"}}\n': 2.3, '",': 2.3, '}",': 4.2, ')",': 3.4, 'EOF': 4.5, '";\n': 0.5}

# Closers after a plain string (no backslash escapes), or after prose.
CLOSE_PLAIN = {'"}}\n': 1.4, '",': 0.3, '}",': 1.2, ')",': 1.0, 'EOF': 3.8, '."': 0.7, '."\n': 0.8,
               '!"': 0.5, '?"': 0.3, '")': 0.35, '",\n': 0.25, '";\n': 0.05}

ESCAPED_QUOTE = '\\",'  # an escaped closing quote inside escaped text: slightly negative


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Value at the newest token. carry = (inside a double-quoted string, its text had a backslash)."""
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    new_doc = len(prefix.token_strings) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    inside, escaped = (False, False) if carry is None or new_doc else carry

    value = 0.0
    if tok == ESCAPED_QUOTE:
        value = -0.9
    elif tok in CLOSE_PLAIN:
        value = CLOSE_ESCAPED.get(tok, 0.0) if escaped else CLOSE_PLAIN[tok]

    # Update the quote state: each double quote toggles inside/outside a string.
    for ch in tok:
        if ch == '"':
            if inside:
                inside = False
            else:
                inside, escaped = True, False
    if inside and '\\' in tok:
        escaped = True
    return (inside, escaped), value

"""layers.1.mlp.down_proj:4278 -- a Hungarian-suffix / Romanian-particle detector.

What it does
  * Strongly NEGATIVE (about -6) on the Hungarian verbal/nominal suffix written as its
    own token inside a word: -ás / -és (and -ása / -ése), as in "fogy|ás" (weight loss),
    "letölt|és" (download), "táplál|ás" (nourishment). Only when the text so far looks
    Hungarian: at least two Hungarian function words ("az", "hogy", "nem", "egy", "van",
    "és", "meg", "még", "ami", "kell") or a Hungarian-only letter (ő, ű).
    The same piece in French, Spanish or Czech text stays near 0.
  * Strongly POSITIVE (about +5.5) on the Romanian subjunctive particle " să"
    ("trebuie să", "puteți să", "permite să").
  * Zero everywhere else.

Why: the component's big activations are rare (about 0.05% of tokens); token identity
alone does not predict them (a per-token table explains nothing held out), but
the language context does. Hungarian and Romanian text carry almost all the variance.
The Hungarian context is tracked in `carry` and reset when the document id changes.
"""

READS = ()

# Verbal/nominal suffix pieces (-ás/-és family) that are negative in Hungarian text.
HU_SUFFIX = {"ás", "és", "ása", "ése"}
# Hungarian function words that mark the text as Hungarian.
HU_WORDS = {" az", " hogy", " nem", " egy", " van", " és", " meg", " még", " ami", " kell"}
# Hungarian-only letters.
HU_LETTERS = "őű"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    # Hungarian evidence seen so far in this document (reset at each document).
    hits = carry[1] if carry is not None and carry[0] == doc else 0
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]

    value = 0.0
    if hits >= 2 and tok in HU_SUFFIX:
        value = -6.0
    elif tok == " să":
        value = 5.5

    if tok in HU_WORDS:
        hits += 1
    if any(c in tok for c in HU_LETTERS):
        hits += 2
    return (doc, hits), value

"""Approximate a document-opening transient, rather than a topic feature.

After an opening run of identical tokens, the first change produces a negative
pulse. It is especially strong in a number, and fades over the next few tokens.
Spacing, capitalization, word continuation and English function words adjust
its size. Initial values use these traits, with a separate value for an
opening end-of-text marker.
Fine token-specific differences and the later background activity are omitted.
"""

READS = ()

FUNCTION_WORDS = set('''
a an the of to in on at by for from with as into onto over under about through
between among without and or but nor yet so if than that which who whose whom
what when where why how this these those it its he him his she her hers they
them their we us our you your i me my be is am are was were been being do does
did have has had will would shall should can could may might must not no all
any some each every both either neither such there here
'''.split())


def traits(token):
    word = token.strip()
    return {
        'digit': word.isdigit(),
        'capital': word.istitle() or word.isupper(),
        'space': token.startswith(' '),
        'unspaced': word.isalpha() and word.islower()
                  and not token.startswith(' '),
        'function': word.lower() in FUNCTION_WORDS,
        'newline': '\n' in token,
        'length': min(len(word), 12) / 12,
        'blank': not word,
        'punctuation': bool(word) and not any(c.isalnum() for c in word),
    }


def initial(token, f):
    if token == '<|endoftext|>':
        return 3.04
    if f['blank']:
        return 0.10
    return (0.12 - 0.50*f['digit'] + 0.31*f['capital']
            - 0.20*f['space'] + 0.20*f['unspaced']
            - 0.20*f['function'] + 0.15*f['length'])


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    f = traits(token)
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        age, first, previous, same = 0, token, token, True
        numeric = f['digit']
    else:
        _, age, first, previous, same, numeric = carry
        same = same and token == first
        age = 0 if same else age + 1
        numeric = numeric and f['digit']
    state = (doc, age, first, token, same, numeric)
    if age == 0:
        return state, initial(token, f)
    if age > 7:
        return state, 0.0
    a = traits(first)
    # Opening-pulse magnitude; the coefficients are fitted on training rows.
    pulse = (-1.30 - .80*a['digit'] + .30*a['capital']
             - .45*a['space'] + .50*a['length']
             + .45*a['punctuation'] - .70*f['digit']
             + .20*f['capital'] + .30*f['unspaced']
             - .45*f['function'] + .45*f['newline']
             + .40*f['length'] + .20*f['punctuation'])
    if age > 1:
        pulse += .15 - 1.30*previous.strip().isdigit()
    fade = (0, 1, .38, .15, .08, .05, .03, .02)[age]
    number_fade = (0, 1, .60, .28, .15, .08, .05, .03)[age]
    value = fade*pulse - 2.30*number_fade*numeric
    return state, float(value)

"""Component layers.1.mlp.down_proj:4279 as a document-opening detector.

It is quiet almost everywhere, but acts on the first few tokens of each document (positions
are counted from the document's first token, restarting at each new document). Its value
is negative and strongest at the second token (about -0.9), weaker at the third (about
-0.3) and fourth (about -0.1), and slightly positive at the first token (about +0.14).
Digits make it more negative: each digit seen so far in the document scales the value
up by one more unit (1 + digits), so a number that opens a document is strongly negative.
Beyond the fourth token it predicts 0.
"""

READS = ()
DIGITS = set("0123456789")
# Base activation by place in the document: index 0 is the document's first token.
BASE = {0: 0.14, 1: -0.94, 2: -0.32, 3: -0.09}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    k, n_digits = carry if carry is not None else (-1, 0)
    if len(prefix.token_ids) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        k, n_digits = -1, 0  # a new document starts here
    k += 1
    s = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if s and all(c in DIGITS for c in s):
        n_digits += 1
    value = BASE.get(k, 0.0) * (1 + n_digits)
    return (k, n_digits), value

"""Document-start detector for layers.1.mlp.down_proj:4281.

This component is a weak, mostly diffuse direction in layer 1's MLP output. Its
clearest, most consistent response is at the first token of each document (the
token right after a document boundary, where a row packs several documents):

- A document's first token pushes the component clearly positive (about +0.4 on
  average) when it is a word, punctuation or symbol.
- A document whose first token is a digit pushes it negative (about -0.25).
- Everywhere else it sits near zero (about -0.015 on average) with small noise
  that no simple token or word class explains.

The program predicts those numbers, with no state carried between positions.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

DOC_START_VALUE = 0.4      # first token of a document that is not a digit
DIGIT_START_VALUE = -0.25  # first token of a document that starts with a digit
ELSEWHERE_VALUE = -0.015   # mean activation at all other positions


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    # The first token of a row, or the first token after a document change.
    first = len(prefix.token_ids) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    if not first:
        return None, ELSEWHERE_VALUE
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()
    if token[:1].isdigit():
        return None, DIGIT_START_VALUE
    return None, DOC_START_VALUE

"""Whitespace-run detector for layers.1.mlp.down_proj:4282.

What it does: this component is silent on almost every token, and fires on
whitespace that sits in front of a line break or inside a run of spaces:

  * A space (or tab, or no-break space) followed by a line break, in one token:
    " \\n" and " \\r\\n" fire hardest (~2.8), other "indent + line break" tokens
    such as "\\t\\n", " \\n\\n" or "  \\n" fire at about 1.6.
  * A lone " " token that directly follows another " " token, i.e. the second
    space of a double space when the tokenizer splits the spaces (typically
    "word  12", "Table  3"): about 2.4.
  * A bare carriage return "\\r" (~0.75) and a no-break space "\\xa0" (~0.4).

Plain newlines ("\\n", "\\n\\n") and ordinary words, digits and punctuation
predict 0. The program is stateless: it reads only the newest token and the one
before it, and only within the same document.
"""

READS = ()

TRAILING_SPACE_BEFORE_BREAK = 2.8  # " \n" and " \r\n"
OTHER_WHITESPACE_BEFORE_BREAK = 1.6  # "\t\n", " \n\n", "  \n", ... (lead with space/tab)
SECOND_OF_DOUBLE_SPACE = 2.4  # " " right after " "
CARRIAGE_RETURN = 0.75  # "\r" alone
NO_BREAK_SPACE = 0.4  # "\xa0" alone


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    same_doc = len(prefix) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2] if same_doc else ""
    if tok == " " and prev == " ":
        return None, SECOND_OF_DOUBLE_SPACE
    if tok in (" \n", " \r\n"):
        return None, TRAILING_SPACE_BEFORE_BREAK
    if tok != "" and tok.strip() == "" and "\n" in tok and tok[0] in (" ", "\t", "\xa0"):
        return None, OTHER_WHITESPACE_BEFORE_BREAK
    if tok == "\r":
        return None, CARRIAGE_RETURN
    if tok == "\xa0":
        return None, NO_BREAK_SPACE
    return None, 0.0

"""Component layers.1.mlp.down_proj:4283: a lexical "operate / record / copy" detector.

It goes negative when the text completed by the newest token contains one of a few
characters or words the model keys on:

  * 営 (Japanese "operate / business", 営業, 運営): by far the strongest;
  * 録 / 录 / 錄 (record: 登録, 録音, 录取, 收录, 目录);
  * 抄 (copy out) and 引用 (quote): the same "copy / cite / record" idea;
  * 營 / 营 (operate / run a business: 经营, 运营);
  * 영 (Korean reading of 映, "reflect / screen": 영상, 상영, 반영; not 영화, "movie");
  * 饮 / 飲 (drink) and 灌 (pour).

Kanji are often split across byte-level tokens: the first pieces of 営 show up as "�", and the
piece that completes the character is where the activation sits. So the program decodes the
text through this token and through the previous one, and reads what this token completes.
Everything else predicts 0.

only part of a longer word ("ing", "into", "info", "information", "instance").

alone. It does not look at context, so it misses the small negative values
of "in" used as a Python/C# loop keyword ("for x in y").

SYLLABLE = re.compile(r"[a-z]{0,2}in[aeiouy]?")
OTHER_SCRIPT = re.compile(r"ин|ین|ين|ın|ín|ін|イン")
NOT_SYLLABLE = {"win", "line", "lin", "sin", "ein"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    if token == "in":
        value = 1.05
    elif token in NOT_SYLLABLE:
        value = 0.0
    elif SYLLABLE.fullmatch(token):
        value = 1.0
    elif len(token) <= 5 and OTHER_SCRIPT.search(token):
        value = 1.5
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return carry, value

"""English compound and affix boundaries, approximated with dictionaries.

A familiar joined spelling crossing a space or hyphen gets a positive score.
Productive bound prefixes (pre-, post-, sub-, etc.) also supply evidence, even
when the following root is unfinished. Underscores and CamelCase prefix
boundaries are also recognized. Some later root pieces are discounted. Most
other tokens receive zero. This deliberately omits arbitrary per-token offsets
and context-specific strengths.
"""
import re
from functools import lru_cache
import wordnet
from wordfreq import top_n_list, zipf_frequency

READS = ()
BOUND_PREFIXES = set('anti auto bi co inter intra micro macro mono multi neo non '
                     'post pre pseudo semi sub super trans tri ultra'.split())
# Ambiguous free words require a visible link; self also forms open compounds.
LINKED_PREFIXES = set('counter cross de dis ex extra half hyper mid over para '
                      'pro quasi re self supra under un'.split())
FUNCTION_WORDS = set('a an the of in on at to for from by with as and or but '
                     'is are be was were it he she they we you i this that '
                     'these those my your his her its our their not no do '
                     'does did have has had can will would could should '
                     'some any every all each more most other much many '
                     'up down out off'.split())
# Dictionary spelling prefixes let an unfinished token count as part of a word.
SPELLINGS = set()
for word in top_n_list('en', 200000):
    if word.isascii() and word.isalpha() and zipf_frequency(word, 'en') >= 1.5:
        SPELLINGS.update(word[:i] for i in range(4, len(word) + 1))


@lru_cache(100000)
def compound_score(left, right, linked, continued):
    bound = left in BOUND_PREFIXES and right not in FUNCTION_WORDS
    value = 0.03 if linked else 0.0
    if bound:
        value += 0.44 if linked else 0.28
        if continued:
            value -= 0.34
    elif right not in FUNCTION_WORDS:
        if linked and left in LINKED_PREFIXES:
            value += 0.27
        elif left == 'self':
            value += 0.35
    if (len(left) >= 3 and len(right) >= 3
            and left not in FUNCTION_WORDS and right not in FUNCTION_WORDS):
        closed = bool(wordnet.parts_of_speech(left + right))
        spelling = left + right in SPELLINGS
        hyphenated = bool(wordnet.parts_of_speech(left + '-' + right))
        value += 0.21 * closed + 0.17 * spelling + 0.10 * hyphenated
        if continued and (closed or spelling):
            value -= 0.16
    return max(0.0, value)


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    tail = carry[1] if carry is not None and carry[0] == doc else ''
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    text = (tail + token)[-100:]
    value = 0.0
    if re.fullmatch(r'[ _-]*[A-Za-z]+', token):
        match = re.search(r'([A-Za-z]+)([ _-]+)([A-Za-z]+)$', text)
        if match:
            left, separator, right = match.groups()
            continued = bool(re.match('[A-Za-z]', token)
                             and re.search('[A-Za-z]$', tail))
            value = compound_score(left.lower(), right.lower(),
                                   bool(separator.strip()), continued)
        # CamelCase can mark the same boundary in identifiers such as subHeader.
        if token[0].isupper():
            match = re.search(r'([A-Za-z]+)$', tail)
            if match:
                pieces = re.findall(r'[A-Z]?[a-z]+|[A-Z]+(?=[A-Z]|$)', match[1])
                left = pieces[-1].lower() if pieces else match[1].lower()
                if left in BOUND_PREFIXES:
                    value += 0.23
    return (doc, text), float(value)

A rough, partial explanation. The component fires mostly on hyphen-led word fragments,
the second half of a word or compound that is split by a hyphen, such as "-pr" in
"post-prandial", "-re" in "geo-referenced", "-less" in "screen-less", "-work" in

a short lowercase word. Hyphen pieces after other words are weakly positive.

It is also negative on the first word of a document, where the model has no context.
Each rule uses its mean activation in the training sample. Everything else is 0.

Most of the component's variance is diffuse: many small positive and negative values on
ordinary word tokens, with signs that depend on context. Simple word-level rules do not
capture it, so this program explains only about 2% of the variance.

def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    toks = prefix.token_strings
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    tok = toks[-1]
    if len(toks) < 2 or docs[-1] != docs[-2]:
        # first token of a document (no preceding context): a 4-8 letter word is negative
        return None, -0.15 if 4 <= len(tok.strip()) <= 8 else 0.0
    prev = toks[-2]

        short_word = prev.startswith(" ") and 2 <= len(prev) - 1 <= 5 and prev[1:].islower()
